stances.claim: The Comelec Second Division under Presiding Commissioner Inting deserves public commendation for following the Comelec Rules of Procedure strictly -- requiring only Petition, Answer, Preliminary Conference, and Memoranda -- and correctly denying petitions-in-intervention, subpoena motions, and face-to-face argument pleas because they would cause unnecessary delay inconsistent with the summary nature of a COC cancellation case.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-commendation framing (publicly praising procedural fidelity as itself an exemplary judicial virtue)

stances.claim: Reyes v. Comelec (Oct. 22, 2013) settles that COC denial-or-cancellation proceedings are 'summary in nature' -- meaning the Division's discretion to dispense with clarificatory hearings and additional intervenor pleadings is doctrinally backed, not procedurally cavalier.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-anchor citation (single case as authoritative warrant for procedural minimalism)

stances.claim: An early decision -- expected between Christmas and New Year -- is good for the parties and general public alike because it puts to rest the pivotal issue of whether Bongbong Marcos and his supporters can continue spending time, resources, and effort in his presidential quest.
stances.rhetorical_move: speedy-resolution-as-public-good framing (resource-conservation argument for the parties AND the electorate)

stances.claim: Cojuangco v. SBN (April 28, 2021) is yet another SC chiding of the Sandiganbayan and PCGG for inordinate delay -- 32+ years without commencing trial proper -- and the long line of dismissed-for-delay precedents (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 15 years) all 'pale in comparison' to what Cojuangco endured, warranting a stronger reason for dismissal.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-delay taxonomy (lining up 9 precedents to show Cojuangco's case as worst-of-class)

stances.claim: There is something biographically uncomfortable about Justice Edgardo L. Delos Santos optionally retiring on June 29, 2021 -- one year ahead of his scheduled June 12, 2022 retirement and two months after writing the Cojuangco ponencia, which was released publicly only this month -- and equally poignant that Eduardo Cojuangco Jr. died on June 16, 2020 without knowing his constitutional vindication.
stances.rhetorical_move: biographical-aside framing (treating personal facts about the ponente and the deceased petitioner as quietly telling)

notable_anecdotes: The expected timing of the Comelec decision -- 'between Christmas and New Year' -- making the COC case a holiday-season cliffhanger and giving the column its anticipatory urgency.

Justice Delos Santos's optional retirement on June 29, 2021 -- one year ahead of schedule and two months after writing the Cojuangco ponencia which itself was 'released publicly only earlier this month' -- the most quietly suggestive single biographical detail in the column, flagged with 'Interestingly' rather than spelled out.

Eduardo M. Cojuangco Jr.'s death on June 16, 2020 'without knowing the vindication of his constitutional rights' -- the most poignant single fact in CJ's invocations of the inordinate-delay doctrine, demonstrating that justice delayed can be justice the litigant never lives to receive.

Estelito P. Mendoza characterized as 'abogado de campanilla' (literally 'bell-ringing lawyer,' a Filipino-Spanish idiom for top-tier counsel) -- used here approvingly, in contrast to Mendoza's role as Bongbong's counsel in the sister-column A166.
The nine-case ascending delay enumeration (3→4→5→6→6→6→7→10→15 years) -- one of CJ's most concentrated single-paragraph precedent walls in his Comelec/Sandiganbayan-watchdog series.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban commends the Commission on Elections' Second Division, headed by Presiding Commissioner Socorro B. Inting, for following the Comelec Rules of Procedure strictly in handling lawyer Theodore O. Te's petition to cancel Bongbong Marcos's COC. He walks the reader through the four required steps -- valid Petition, Answer, Preliminary Conference by the Clerk of the Division, and Memoranda by both parties -- noting that any clarificatory hearing is discretionary and that under Reyes v. Comelec (October 22, 2013) the proceeding is 'summary in nature.' The Division therefore correctly denied all petitions-in-intervention, subpoena motions, and face-to-face argument pleas, granted both parties only five days to file Memoranda, and deemed the case submitted thereafter; an early decision between Christmas and New Year is good for the parties and public alike because it puts to rest whether Bongbong should continue spending time and resources on his presidential quest. Panganiban then pivots to praise a parallel Supreme Court decision, Cojuangco v. SBN (April 28, 2021, released only this month), which chided the Sandiganbayan and PCGG for letting Eduardo M. Cojuangco Jr.'s ill-gotten wealth cases pend for over 32 years without commencing trial -- citing nine precedents (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, and 15-year delays) that all 'pale in comparison.' He closes with two biographical asides flagged as 'Interestingly' and 'sadly': the ponente Justice Edgardo L. Delos Santos optionally retired on June 29, 2021, one year ahead of schedule and two months after writing the decision; and Cojuangco himself 'passed away on June 16, 2020' without knowing the vindication of his constitutional rights.
